name: Berkson's paradox
statement: Two conditions that are unrelated in the population can look related inside a hospital sample, because being in the sample already requires having one of them.
meaning: This is a property of a sample rather than a habit of a mind. It is one species of selection bias, entry 82, alongside survivorship bias, entry 8, where the filter is survival rather than admission. Suppose two illnesses each raise the chance of being admitted to hospital, and are independent in the general population. Among admitted patients, someone without the first illness is more likely to have the second, because something had to get them through the door. The two now correlate, negatively or positively depending on the admission rates, and nothing in the ward register says so. Modern causal inference gives the mechanism a name: admission is a collider, a variable that both illnesses point into, and restricting a study to the admitted patients conditions on it. The error is not in the reasoning applied to the data. The data were assembled by a filter that both variables helped to operate.

origin.note: "Limitations of the application of fourfold table analysis to hospital data", Biometrics Bulletin 2(3), 47 to 53, reprinted in the International Journal of Epidemiology in 2014. Berkson preferred the word 'paradox' for it, according to Sackett. The name Berkson's bias, and the broader definition covering every cause of differential admission, came later.

evidence: Berkson's paper argues that the fourfold table borrowed from experimental work does not carry the same meaning when its rows come from a hospital. Its opening pages, free to read at the 2014 reprint, set the laboratory design of an experimental group against a control. Berkson then observes that the statistical fourfold table came into authority because it looks equivalent to that design, and lists the indices used to read correlation off it: Pearson's product-moment coefficient, Yule's index of association and the chi-square test. The rest of the paper, including its numerical illustration, could not be read here on 21 September 2026. JSTOR and Elsevier returned bot challenges rather than paywalls, Oxford Academic states that access to the reprint is denied and offers 24-hour purchase, and Europe PMC's free-PDF pointer to the reprint is refused while Unpaywall reports the reprint closed. Snoep and colleagues, who read it, report that Berkson built the example so that in the source population cholecystitis was unassociated with diabetes and with refractive errors, and the hospitalisation probabilities of the three diseases were independent. The first empirical demonstration came 32 years later. Roberts, Spitzer, Delmore and Sackett used household interviews covering both illness and recent hospital use, and Sackett printed two of their tables in 1979. Among 2,784 people in the general population, the relative odds of disease of the bones and organs of movement given respiratory disease were 1.06. Among the 257 of them who had been in hospital in the previous six months, the same relative odds were 4.06. A second pair runs the other way: fatigue given prior allergic or metabolic disease showed relative odds of 1.89 in the general population and 0.37 in the hospitalised subset. Those two pairs come from a larger exercise. Snoep and colleagues report that it drew on three household surveys and examined 28 disease-disease associations, with a spurious association found for most of them among the hospitalised, along with 48 drug-disease associations of which nine showed significant differences. Sackett catalogued the effect as admission rate bias, one of nine biases he discussed out of the 35 biases of sampling and measurement his catalogue then held. The modern treatment is quantitative. Munafo, Tilling, Taylor, Evans and Davey Smith simulated an intended population of 9,000,000 with no association between an allele score and an outcome, and a selected sample of about 500,000. With an odds ratio of 1.5 for missingness per standard deviation of phenotype and of outcome, and a correlation of 0.1 between allele score and phenotype, 89 of 100 simulated 95% intervals contained the true value of zero. In the same paper, higher body mass index predicted lower odds of staying in the ALSPAC birth cohort. The odds ratio for retention was 0.85 per standard deviation of pre-pregnancy body mass index among 11,319 mothers, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.88.

examples.tag: The admitted class where two strengths look opposed
examples.text: A university takes pupils who are either strong academically or strong at sport, and either alone is enough to get in. Inside the admitted year group the two look inversely related, because a weak athlete must have got in on marks. Across all applicants they are unrelated.

Kindness and good looks are roughly independent among everyone you might have met, and either one is enough to earn a first date. Among the people you actually dated the two appear to trade off, and the trade-off was made by the filter rather than by the world.

A service takes calls from people in debt or in poor health, and either qualifies someone for help. Among the callers, debt and illness look linked. Any counsellor reading the caseload as evidence of a link in the town is reading the admission rule back to themselves.

replication.headline: The 1978 household demonstration is not the only one. A Montreal study in 2020 found the childhood-abuse and depression association stronger in a specialist psychiatric sample, on an odds ratio whose interval reaches close to 1.
replication.detail: Laliberte, Giguere, Potvin and Lesage compared 860 people with depression from the Canadian Community Health Survey against 207 from the Signature biobank, which recruits at the emergency department of a university mental health centre in Montreal. Both counts are analysed rather than recruited samples. Of 25,113 people interviewed for the survey, 21,506 were of eligible age and 1,162 reported an episode of major depression; 860 remained after exclusions for bipolar disorder and antipsychotic medication. The biobank's 1,120 participants fell to 1,073 on age, to 353 with a depressive or mood disorder diagnosis, and to 207 after excluding comorbid bipolar disorder or psychotic symptoms. Any childhood abuse was reported by 65.7% of respondents who had been hospitalised for psychiatric treatment or had seen a psychiatrist, 95% CI 59.6% to 71.8%, against 49% of depressed respondents using no services, 95% CI 41.0% to 57.1%. Adjusted for sex, age and comorbid substance use disorder, contact with a psychiatrist or a psychiatric hospital carried an odds ratio of 1.93 for any child abuse, 95% CI 1.06 to 3.53, and membership of the biobank an odds ratio of 1.82, 95% CI 1.16 to 2.86. The first interval runs down to 1.06, so that estimate is marginal. The reference group is depressed respondents who used no mental health services. De Ron, Fried and Epskamp ran two simulation studies on a network built from a dataset of 2,807 patients diagnosed with major depression. Their abstract reports that higher cut-offs on the symptom sum-score went with worse recovery of the network structure, and that selection reduced recovery by inducing negative connections between the items.

study.cite: Laliberte, V., Giguere, C.-E., Potvin, S., & Lesage, A. (2020). Berkson's bias in biobank sampling in a specialised mental health care setting: a comparative cross-sectional study. BMJ Open, 10(7), e035088.

limits: Berkson's paradox is not an experimental effect. There is no protocol to re-run and no effect size to compare across labs. Given two causes of selection, the selected sample is distorted, and that follows from probability rather than being tested. What can be tested is whether real admission rates behave the way the model assumes, and there the record is not one-sided. Feinstein, Walter and Horwitz analysed patterns of hospitalisation and case-control selection algebraically. They report that the bias is avoided if both cases and controls are chosen from the community, or if the hospitalisation rate for the control condition is zero. Berkson's arithmetic treats each condition's effect on admission as independent and additive. Feinstein and colleagues argue that two conditions arriving together may act on the examining physician's decisions synergistically, and that those decisions may matter more than the probabilities Berkson described. Sartwell wrote in 1974, quoted by Sackett, that the practical importance of the bias had not been established. Snoep and colleagues reached a similar view in 2014, concluding that Berkson's fallacy has likely had very limited impact on the findings of epidemiological studies. Levy and Kezios reviewed the question in 2025, keeping 33 of 5,508 articles and 12 of 205 textbooks. Among the sources whose primary focus was collider bias, 37% said the magnitude could be large or small, against 67% of the sources focused on selection bias. Almost half of the collider bias sources said the bias has only a small impact on observed associations. Whether people reason wrongly when a sample has been filtered this way is a different question from whether the filter distorts the sample. A search of Europe PMC and of the open web on 21 September 2026 located no experiment testing it.
misreadings: Berkson's 1946 argument rests on a constructed example rather than on a body of hospital records. Snoep, Morabia, Hernandez-Diaz, Hernan and Vandenbroucke, who read the paper, describe a hospital estimating the association between cholecystitis and diabetes, with diabetic patients as cases and patients carrying refractive errors as controls. Berkson chose the numbers so that cholecystitis was unassociated with either of the other two conditions in the source population, and so that the three hospitalisation probabilities were independent. The association appeared among the hospitalised alone. The costly confusion is with confounding, because the remedies point in opposite directions. A confounder is controlled by adjusting for it; a collider is turned into a bias by adjusting for it, so the reflex that fixes the first causes the second. Westreich adds that restricting to one level of a collider is the same move as analysing only complete cases, which makes Berkson's bias a model of bias from missing data. A third error is treating the label as a verdict. Griffith and colleagues found that of 486,967 UK Biobank participants only 1,410 then had COVID-19 test data, and that 811 of 2,556 measured characteristics, 32%, were associated with having been tested at a false discovery rate below 0.05. That establishes selection, not the direction or size of any resulting error. Their sensitivity analysis on the reported protective association between smoking and COVID-19 assumed a smoking prevalence of 0.27 in the general population and 0.05 in the sample. Over that parameter space, 40% of all possible combinations produce an artefactual two-fold protective or risk association. Forty per cent of a parameter space is a warning, not a refutation of the smoking result.

sources.text: Berkson, J. (1946). Limitations of the application of fourfold table analysis to hospital data. Biometrics Bulletin, 2(3), 47. Crossref confirms author, journal, volume, issue and June 1946; Sackett's 1979 reference list gives the page range as 47 to 53. Full text not obtained: JSTOR returned a bot challenge on 21 September 2026.

Berkson, J. (2014). Limitations of the Application of Fourfold Table Analysis to Hospital Data. International Journal of Epidemiology, 43(2), 511-515. The 2014 reprint. Opening pages read free at Oxford Academic on 21 September 2026; the same page states that access to the remainder is denied and offers 24-hour purchase. Europe PMC lists a free PDF of it and that link is refused; Unpaywall reports the reprint closed.

Sackett, D. L. (1979). Bias in analytic research. Journal of Chronic Diseases, 32(1-2), 51-63. Full text read from the James Lind Library scan on 21 September 2026. Tables 2 and 3, adapted from Roberts et al., carry the 1.06, 4.06, 1.89 and 0.37 figures; the text gives the 35-bias catalogue, the nine biases discussed, Berkson's preference for 'paradox' and the Sartwell quotation.

Roberts, R. S., Spitzer, W. O., Delmore, T., & Sackett, D. L. (1978). An empirical demonstration of Berkson's bias. Journal of Chronic Diseases, 31(2), 119-128. PubMed holds no abstract for it, confirmed at the E-utilities record on 21 September 2026, and Unpaywall reports it closed. The figures used here are Sackett's 1979 reprinting of its tables; its scope is reported at one remove by Snoep and colleagues.

Feinstein, A. R., Walter, S. D., & Horwitz, R. I. (1986). An analysis of Berkson's bias in case-control studies. Journal of Chronic Diseases, 39(7), 495-504. The claims used here are read off the abstract, fetched from PubMed's E-utilities record on 21 September 2026. Full text not obtained: ScienceDirect and jclinepi.com returned bot challenges, and the Internet Archive copy is blocked by this session's egress policy. OpenAlex and Unpaywall mark it open at the publisher, and the DOI resolves to an Elsevier landing page with no free file.

Munafo, M. R., Tilling, K., Taylor, A. E., Evans, D. M., & Davey Smith, G. (2018). Collider scope: when selection bias can substantially influence observed associations. International Journal of Epidemiology, 47(1), 226-235. Published online 27 September 2017. Full text read as JATS XML from Europe PMC, PMC5837306, on 21 September 2026; Table 1 carries the simulation coverage counts and the ALSPAC retention figures sit in the text.

Griffith, G. J., Morris, T. T., Tudball, M. J., et al. (2020). Collider bias undermines our understanding of COVID-19 disease risk and severity. Nature Communications, 11, 5749. Full text read as JATS XML from Europe PMC, PMC7665028, on 21 September 2026.

Westreich, D. (2012). Berkson's bias, selection bias, and missing data. Epidemiology, 23(1), 159-164. Full text of the NIH author manuscript read from PubMed Central, PMC3237868, on 21 September 2026. Source for the analogy between restricting to one level of a collider and a complete-case analysis.

Snoep, J. D., Morabia, A., Hernandez-Diaz, S., Hernan, M. A., & Vandenbroucke, J. P. (2014). Commentary: A structural approach to Berkson's fallacy and a guide to a history of opinions about it. International Journal of Epidemiology, 43(2), 515-521. Full text read at PubMed Central, PMC3997377, on 21 September 2026; Europe PMC and NCBI refuse machine download of it, so the passages used here were read twice, and the description of Berkson's example was confirmed against the free extract at Oxford Academic. Source for what Berkson's example contains, for the scope of Roberts et al. and for the authors' judgement of the fallacy's impact.

Laliberte, V., Giguere, C.-E., Potvin, S., & Lesage, A. (2020). Berkson's bias in biobank sampling in a specialised mental health care setting: a comparative cross-sectional study. BMJ Open, 10(7), e035088. Full text read as JATS XML from Europe PMC, PMC7380858, on 21 September 2026. Table 2 carries the odds ratios of 1.93 and 1.82; the participant flow from 25,113 and 1,120 down to 860 and 207 is in the methods.

Published online 4 December 2019. The abstract, read in full from the Crossref record on 21 September 2026, carries the 2,807-patient dataset, the two simulation studies and the finding on cut-offs and negative connections. Full text not obtained; Unpaywall reports it closed and Cambridge Core holds it behind subscription.

Levy, N. S., & Kezios, K. L. (2025). The Same but Different?: A Systematic Review of the Impact of Selection and Collider Bias on Internal Validity. Epidemiology, 36(4), 473-481. Full text of the author manuscript read from PubMed Central, PMC12122217, on 21 September 2026; the counts of retained articles and textbooks and the percentages used here are in the abstract and the results.
